procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a Writ Petition (Civil) No. 324 of 2020 under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, seeking directions to the Union of India and all States and Union Territories to implement provisions of the Act of 1993 and Act of 2013. The Supreme Court is hearing the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether a differentiation can be held unconstitutional without a challenge to the statute.

facts: An argument was made that the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and Their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, treats 'manual scavenging' and 'hazardous cleaning' differently.

The plea contended that this differentiation violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India because there is no rational basis for providing rehabilitation for manual scavengers but not for hazardous cleaners.
The court noted that it was not presented with a formal legal challenge to the provisions of the statute itself.
law: A court cannot declare a statutory differentiation to be unconstitutional unless the specific provisions of the statute creating that differentiation are formally challenged.
application: The court acknowledged the argument that the different treatment of the two categories of workers might violate Article 14.
However, the court determined that its ability to rule on the constitutionality of this differentiation was dependent on a direct challenge to the law.
Since no such challenge was made in this case, the court could not proceed to examine the constitutional validity of the distinction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the differentiation was unconstitutional, reasoning that it could not make such a determination because the statute itself had not been challenged.

issue.issue_text: Whether a valid survey was conducted despite the failure to prepare a provisional list, call for objections, and publish a final list as required by the statute.

facts: The government claimed that surveys were conducted in 2013 and 2018.
However, no provisional list was prepared as required by Section 11(4) of the Act.
No objections were called for or decided upon as mandated by Section 11(5).
No final list was published as required by Section 11(6).
The institutions legally required to conduct the survey, namely the District and State Level Survey Committees, were not constituted or were not functioning at the time of the alleged surveys.
law: The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and Their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, and its associated Rules prescribe a specific and mandatory procedure for conducting surveys.
This procedure includes preparing a provisional list, calling for objections, and publishing a final list.

There is an established legal principle that "where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all and that other methods of performance are necessarily forbidden."
application: The court applied the legal principle that the specific method prescribed by the Act and Rules must be followed exclusively.

Since the mandatory steps of preparing a provisional list, calling for objections, and publishing a final list were not followed, the court determined the surveys were not conducted in the legally required manner.
The court found that a valid survey was impossible from the outset because the very committees entrusted with the duty to conduct and oversee the surveys were not in place.
The court also noted that it had previously found the 2013 survey to be insufficient in the 'Safai Karamchari Andolan' case, and therefore the government could not rely on it again.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that a valid survey was conducted. The court reasoned that the surveys were invalid because they failed to follow the mandatory procedures laid out in the statute, specifically the requirements to prepare a provisional list, call for objections, and publish a final list. Additionally, the surveys were fundamentally flawed because the legally required committees responsible for conducting them had not been constituted or were not functioning.

cases.case_name: Safai Karamchari Andolan and Others vs. Union of India & Ors
cases.principle: As a precedent where the Court had previously addressed the same subject matter, analyzed the provisions of the 2013 Act, and issued directions for its implementation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all, and other methods of performance are necessarily forbidden.
obiter: Articles 15, 17, 23, and 24 of the Constitution form an emancipatory code, creating a fundamental right for oppressed classes to move to alternative, dignified employment.
Without a challenge to the statutory provisions, a differentiation created by the statute cannot be held unconstitutional.
Hazardous cleaning amounts to forced labour under Article 23 of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's reasoning for the first issue is that a court cannot rule on the constitutionality of a differentiation created by a statute unless the statute itself is formally challenged. For a claim of unconstitutional differentiation under Article 14 to succeed, the underlying legal provision must be the subject of the challenge. The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for the second issue concerning the validity of the survey.
legal_tests_applied: Article 14 of the Constitution of India: A differentiation created by a statute cannot be held unconstitutional without a direct challenge to the provisions of that statute.
why_appellant_lost: The court did not address the merits of the differentiation claim because the petitioner failed to challenge the underlying statute that created the differentiation.
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on the first issue because the court determined it could not proceed to rule the differentiation unconstitutional due to the petitioner's procedural failure to challenge the statute itself.
policy_considerations: In a country like India where there is so much poverty and unemployment and there is no equality of bargaining power, a contract of service may appear on its face voluntary but it may, in reality, be involuntary, because while entering into the contract, the employee, by reason of his economically helpless condition, may have been faced with Hobson’s choice, either to starve or to submit to the exploitative terms dictated by the powerful employer.

It would be a travesty of justice to hold the employee in such a case to the terms of the contract and to compel him to serve the employer even though he may not wish to do so. That would aggravate the inequality and injustice from which the employee even otherwise suﬀers on account of his economically disadvantaged position and lend the authority of law to the exploitation of the poor helpless employee by the economically powerful employer.
Article 23 therefore says that no one shall be forced to provide labour or service against his will, even though it be under a contract of service.

The defence of any contractor or authority that a hazardous worker had entered into a sewer or septic tank voluntarily without any protective gear or cleaning devices, would not stand constitutional scrutiny.

The lack of mechanization to clean sewer lines or septic tanks is against the statutory as well as constitutional mandate. Cleaning devices as well as protective gear must be provided to ensure that manual cleaning of sewers and septic tanks is not done.
